bar.angle_ref: Wegg & Gerhard 2013, MNRAS 435, 1874 (box/peanut bulge, angle from the Sun-centre line); the long bar outside the bulge is at 28-33 deg (Wegg, Gerhard & Portail 2015)
bar.long_bar_scale_height_ref: Wegg, Gerhard & Portail 2015 (super-thin part concentrated towards the bar ends)
bar.bulge_axis_ratio_ref: Wegg & Gerhard 2013, box/peanut bulge, as quoted in Bland-Hawthorn & Gerhard 2016, ARA&A 54, 529, sec. 4.2.1
bar.near_end: first Galactic quadrant (positive longitude, positive beta)

disc.thin_ref: Bland-Hawthorn & Gerhard 2016, ARA&A 54, 529, sec. 5.1 (height ~300 pc to within 20%, Juric et al. 2008)
disc.thick_ref: Bland-Hawthorn & Gerhard 2016, sec. 5.1.3 and 5.2.2 (thick disc defined by high [alpha/Fe])

dust_disc.profile: exp(-R / scale_length) * sech^2(z / h(R)); h = base for R <= flare_start, base + flare * (R - flare_start) beyond (~188 pc at the Sun). Hole inside 0.5 R0: density there = density(0.5 R0) * exp(-((R/R0 - 0.5)^2) / 0.25^2)
dust_disc.ref: Drimmel & Spergel 2001, ApJ 556, 181, eq. 13-14 and Table 1 (values assume R0 = 8 kpc)

milky_way.about: Our galaxy: a barred spiral, its stars in a thin disc wound into four major arms around a central bar. We see it from inside, as the band of the Milky Way across the sky, so its shape has to be pieced together from distances to its stars and gas. Drawn here from published measurements; the points themselves are scattered to match, not real stars, except the rings: real masers at their measured distances.
milky_way.maser: A maser is the microwave version of a laser (Microwave Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation). Around a newborn massive star, water and methanol molecules in the gas are energised by the star's heat or by gas it blows out, and then beam out radio waves at one exact frequency, very bright and from a spot smaller than the Solar System. Bright and tiny, they can be tracked by radio telescopes spread across the Earth, working as one Earth-sized telescope, which measure their parallax: the small yearly shift as Earth goes round the Sun, which gives their true distance through the dust. A few masers are not newborn stars but massive stars late in life (red supergiants such as VY Canis Majoris), with masers in their swollen outer layers.
milky_way.maser_short: Masers: molecules in the gas round a star that beam out bright, pinpoint radio waves (a laser for microwaves), so radio telescopes can measure their distance through the dust. Mostly round newborn massive stars.
milky_way.maser_ref: Reid et al. 2019, ApJ 885, 131, sec. 2 and Table 1 (methanol and water masers; VLBA, VERA, EVN and LBA parallaxes)
milky_way.orbit_speed_ref: Reid et al. 2019, ApJ 885, 131, Table 3 fit A5: circular speed plus the Sun's own motion, Θ0 + V⊙ = 247 ± 4 km/s

facts.label: New stars
facts.ref: Licquia & Newman 2015, ApJ 806, 96, as quoted by Bland-Hawthorn & Gerhard 2016

facts.label: Arms
facts.value: four major arms, wound at about 10° on average
facts.ref: Reid et al. 2019, sec. 8 (pitch angles weighted by segment length)

history.text: Morgan, Sharpless and Osterbrock trace the first three arm segments near the Sun from distances to young hot stars and the glowing gas around them: today's Sagittarius-Carina, Local and Perseus arms.
Oort, Kerr and Westerhout map the whole disc in the radio glow of hydrogen gas (21 cm) and draw the Galaxy as a spiral.
Radio telescopes spanning the Earth measure parallaxes (the true distances) of about 200 masers, mostly round newborn massive stars, pinning down where the arms are.
history.ref: Reid et al. 2019, ApJ 885, 131 (BeSSeL Survey and VERA)

centre.name: Galactic Centre (Sgr A*)
centre.about: The middle of the Milky Way, behind thick dust towards Sagittarius: Sagittarius A*, a black hole of 4.3 million Suns, at the heart of the bar. Stars there race round it on orbits of a few years to decades, which is how it was weighed.
centre.mass_ref: GRAVITY Collaboration 2021, A&A 647, A59 (4.297 ± 0.013 million Suns, fitted with R0 = 8,275 pc)

facts.label: Closest star
facts.value: S2 goes round every 16 years, passing 120 AU from it at 7,650 km/s (May 2018)

facts.label: First image
facts.value: 2022, Event Horizon Telescope: a bright ring 51.8 microarcseconds across, the black hole's shadow
facts.ref: Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration 2022, ApJL 930, L12

facts.label: Found
facts.value: 1974, as a tiny bright radio source, by Balick and Brown

facts.label: Nobel Prize
facts.value: Physics 2020: Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez, for showing it is a supermassive compact object
facts.ref: nobelprize.org, The Nobel Prize in Physics 2020

objects.name: Sagittarius B2
objects.note: One of the most massive molecular clouds in the Galaxy, near the centre.

Norma-Outer.about: A major arm that starts at the end of the bar as the Norma arm, wraps round the far side of the centre, and returns as the Outer arm, the farthest one beyond the Sun. A new distance to S269 showed the Outer arm flattening into a near circle past the anticentre (the direction away from the centre).

objects.name: S269
objects.note: A nebula far out in the Outer arm; its new distance revealed the arm's kink.

objects.name: V838 Monocerotis
objects.note: A star that brightened 10,000-fold in 2002, lighting up a famous light echo in the dust around it (Bond et al. 2003, Nature 422, 405).

Scutum-Centaurus-OSC.about: A major arm that starts near the bar, winds out through Scutum and Centaurus, passes behind the centre and comes back on the far side of the Galaxy as the Outer Scutum-Centaurus arm. A single star-forming region beyond the centre, G007.47+00.05, ties the two pieces into one arm.
Scutum-Centaurus-OSC.ref: Reid et al. 2019, sec. 3.2.2 (Sanna et al. 2017)

objects.name: W43
objects.note: A huge molecular cloud complex forming stars fast, where the arm may meet the end of the bar (Nguyen-Luong et al. 2011, A&A 529, A41).

objects.name: G007.47+00.05
objects.note: The most distant maser measured here, beyond the centre: it links Scutum-Centaurus to its far side.

Sagittarius-Carina.about: The next major arm in towards the centre. It has a sharp kink: almost circular towards Sagittarius and Aquila, it winds out steeply (about 17°) through Carina, a bend first suggested by Burton and Shane in 1970.

objects.name: W51
objects.note: One of the largest star-forming complexes in the Galaxy.

Perseus.about: The next major arm out from the Sun. Long counted one of the Milky Way's two dominant arms, with Scutum-Centaurus, but young massive stars are plentiful only towards Cassiopeia and Perseus: further in, star formation fades for about 8 kpc (26,000 ly) along it, and past the anticentre it may die out.

objects.name: W3(OH)
objects.note: In the W3 star-forming complex, next to the Heart Nebula in Cassiopeia.

objects.name: NGC 7538
objects.note: A nebula with young massive stars, in Cepheus.

objects.name: W49N
objects.note: One of the most luminous star-forming regions in the Galaxy, on the far side of its arm.

Local.about: The Sun's own arm, also called the Orion Arm or Orion Spur. A short segment between the Sagittarius-Carina and Perseus arms, full of young massive stars, that does not wind all the way round the Galaxy like the four major arms.
Local.ref: Reid et al. 2019, sec. 3.3 (mapped by Xu et al. 2013, 2016)

objects.name: Orion Nebula (Orion KL)
objects.note: The nearest place where massive stars are forming.

objects.name: DR21 (Cygnus X)
objects.note: In Cygnus X, one of the biggest star-forming complexes near the Sun.

objects.name: VY Canis Majoris
objects.note: A red hypergiant, one of the largest stars known.
